content.thinking:
I'm planning the kraken design in an Overwatch-inspired style: a bulbous mantle rising from the water with glowing eyes and spread tentacles, using crisp color-blocked panels with a deep navy-purple body and a cyan accent glow.

I'm scaling the creature so the mantle stands about 3m tall with tentacles spanning roughly 8m, resting their tips against the floor to suggest contact with water. Now I'm working out the skeleton: a spine chain running up through the mantle, a separate jaw structure, and eight tentacle chains radiating from the body base, each built as tapering joint sequences.

Adding head and eye placement...

For the eyelid, I'll use a torus ring around the iris in dark armor colour plus a brow plate extrusion. For the jaw, I'm setting up a beak with upper and lower cone-shaped parts attached to head and jaw bones, positioning them at the front-bottom of the head with appropriate joint placements. Then I'm working out the tentacle arrangement, spacing eight arms radially around the head with calculated angles.

Now I'm figuring out the tentacle paths themselves -- each one starts near the head, curves outward and down to the floor, lies along the ground with S-shaped wiggles out to a good distance, then curls up at the tip, with the radius tapering from thick at the base to thin at the tip and the path height tuned so the tube just grazes the floor without clipping through it.

I'm blending the vertical motion with smoothstep curves so arms dip near the root before rising, factoring in tube radius and body sphere dimensions to make sure the tentacle roots plausibly connect into the kraken's body without poking through oddly.

Now I'm setting up the tentacle chains using Catmull-Rom paths parented to the body, then sweeping tubes along each chain with a radius function that tapers over t and rounded caps, assigning colors like deep indigo for the body with contrasting underside tones for that Overwatch-style color blocking.

I'm layering a countershade paint between indigo and lavender, then adding periodic banding by checking if a scaled parameter snaps near integer values to darken those ring segments for a tentacle sucker pattern.

For the glow accents, I'm thinking of placing small glowing cyan spheres along the dorsal line of each tentacle using an "along" helper that walks a sweep path and sticks embedded shapes at intervals.

For suckers, I'll add rings of lavender with dark cup centers along the underside of each arm, using angled sampling so the three raised arms show a full row of suckers while the floor-lying arms only get them along the side angles to avoid clipping into the ground.

Now I'm moving to the mantle's armor plating, planning overlapping shell shapes and a dorsal crest fin extruded along the back profile.

I'm also sketching lateral fins at the mantle top and defining the mantle's path points and radii at each knot, then checking that the swept shape reaches a reasonable total height with joints placed at the path knots for the chain.

Still shaping fin geometry...

Actually using fin.local() for the rod points is cleaner since it handles the frame's own axes automatically, so I'll place glow rods along the fin's front face with explicit bone/joint references rather than computing raw vectors myself.

For the dorsal crest, I'm placing spikes along the mantle sweep using the tube's own orientation—since the mantle leans back, using the tube's "0" side naturally gives the dorsal-facing spikes without extra math.

For armor, I'm adding ring-shaped plate bands cut across the mantle at a few joint locations, using closed catmull sweeps to form teal accent ridges circling the body at each point.

Writing paint/mottle logic...

Still defining mantle path and joints...

I'm checking whether a flat iris disc placed inside the eyeball sphere actually stays within the sphere's radius, and finding it pokes outside, so I'm reconsidering using a textured sphere for the eyeball instead, mapping the iris onto its surface via UV coordinates rather than a separate disc.

Adding a brow-plate for the eyelid, shaping it like a chunky armored box aligned with the gaze direction and positioned above and slightly forward of the eye socket.

For colors, I'm settling on a deep navy-purple body with pale bone/steel armor plates and a single strong glowing cyan-teal accent for contrast, rather than orange. Now I'm planning the armor plate layout: brow plates, a beak guard, and overlapping shell plates along the mantle.

Adding dorsal armor plates...

Adding cuff rings...

Now I'm working out the beak geometry—shaping the upper cone to aim forward and downward from the head, figuring out the direction vector and center placement so the tip points correctly.

I'm also planning the arm angles around the body, spacing the eight arms at varying degrees from the front axis so they don't collide with the beak.

For the beak itself, I'm shaping a hooked upper cone and a smaller lower cone to form the mandibles, plus considering a small glowing sphere inside the mouth for a bioluminescent effect.

Now I'm thinking through the skeleton structure: adding eye joints parented to the head with gaze direction, fan-like fin joints off the mantle, and planning dorsal crest spikes along the back.

Scattering small barnacle cones across the upper mantle surface for texture, while deciding to skip seaweed cards and water-ring details to keep the kraken focused on the rising-from-water pose.

Tallying up the total part count across body, plates, spikes, barnacles, fins, eyes, beak, and arm suckers lands around 300 parts, with the sucker cylinders contributing the bulk of triangles but staying well within budget. Skipping the webbed membrane between arms to keep things simpler, and moving on to setting up the chain helper for the tentacle paths.

Working out naming conventions for the arm joints so they don't collide—using letter-based prefixes per arm with sequential indices, tagged with a "tentacle" role, and setting up seed values to compute each arm's path points.

Now I'm defining the eight arm positions by their angle offsets around the body, spacing them so the front and back pairs don't overlap given their radius, then assigning per-arm length and height-raise values.

Writing arm point generation code...

Still building the arm sweep geometry...

Adding glow dots along the dorsal line and double-checking that only the actually-used imports are included to avoid unused-import errors.

I'm setting up the meta export with name, description, style, and commit info, then writing the fin extrusion logic for both sides, defining each fin's position, orientation vectors, thickness, bevel, and bone binding.

Still writing outline points...

Working out which side faces up for s=-1 gives a downward axis, so I'm determining rib placement on the top face using sign of the fin's local y-axis, then adding three short cyan rods near the top edge of the fin as decorative ribs.

I'm checking each rib's endpoints against the outline boundary to make sure they stay inside the fin shape, then defining the paint function for the fin that blends indigo and teal based on position along its length.

Now I'm setting up the fin joints attached to the mantle's second joint, positioning them symmetrically on each side with directional vectors for the fan role. Then I'm starting the mantle sweep with a tapering radius profile for a smooth organic shape.

Using 10 sweep sides for a smoother body, I work out the dorsal plate placement by sampling points along the mantle's curve where it leans backward, planning five overlapping scute plates spaced along that back section.

Still writing plate geometry...

Still placing spikes and plates...

Now I'm picking colors for the plates and trim, using a countershaded pale blue-violet with darker shadow tones, and deciding to skip extra snout armor and face mask details to keep things simple.

Scattering barnacles across the mantle surface, filtering hits by normal and position to avoid overlapping the back plates, then shaping them as small embedded cones. Now moving on to setting up the head joint and eyes.

Setting up the jaw joint...

Lower beak base sits fine inside the body too. I'm picking a pale bone color for the beak with dark contrast tones, and placing a small glow sphere inside the mouth area. Now I'm setting up the eyes, positioning mirrored eyeball spheres with gaze direction and color.

Writing eye geometry code...

Writing iris SVG layers...

I'm defining a tight color palette under 64 colors—indigo tones, teal highlights, bone and sucker shades—then starting the skin paint function that layers mottling and countershading onto the base indigo for the creature's texture.

Still writing paint logic... checking how arm rings, mantle sectors, and seam glow loops will sample from this skin paint, and whether chain points can serve as valid frame inputs for sweeping surfaces along the mantle.

I'm checking ring placement against the eye bumps, since the loop at that height would cut through the protruding eyeball. I'll shift the rings higher, past the brow line, settling on t values around .36 and .46 to clear the geometry.

Now I'm repositioning the plate centers so they don't collide with the glow rings—spacing five plates evenly from t=.55 to .97, and checking that the topmost plate near the cap still has enough radius to fit cleanly.

For the plates themselves, flat boxes wrapped onto the cylinder create a visible gap at the edges since the chord doesn't match the curve, so I'm narrowing the width to around .9r to minimize the float and embedding them slightly to compensate. I'll also add a small glowing sphere tip at the end of each arm, attaching it to the last joint in the bone chain.

I'm checking that the tip and the lying arms stay just above the floor level without clipping through, and tuning the wiggle animation so raised arms sway less than extended ones.

Now I'm working through the coordinate math for positioning joints around the body, converting angles from degrees to radians, and setting up the loop placement for arm cuffs along each limb's centerline using the sweep surface. Writing the smoothing function...

Working out the brow geometry's tilt direction—figuring out which way the up vector should lean so the inner end of the eyebrow sits lower for an angry slant, tracing through how the local X axis derives from the cross product of the up and direction vectors.

Good, that's settled. Now I'm working out the arm attachment, sucker placement along each sweep, and the glow dot positions before writing the final code.
